55: One must wave the lulav and etrog six times each day, corresponding to the six directions of the universe: The first time one waves is when one recites the blessing. One waves the lulav when one recites the first and the last verses, hodu. Explanation: The first hodu is a single wave at the beginning, and the second hodu is toward the end, following baruch haba. One waves it twice because we recite this verse (hodu) twice. One waves the lulav and etrog when one recites Ana Adonai hoshia na (אָֽנָּא יְיְ הוֹשִֽׁיעָה נָּא) twice. This makes six times. The Baal HaMinhagot (HaManhig)19Authored by Abraham ben Nathan was a Provençal rabbi and scholar of the 12th–13th centuries. writes that the reason we wave the lulav and etrog when saying Ana Adonai hoshia na (“Please God, save us, please”) and not when reciting Ana Adonai hatzlicha na (“Please God, rescue us, please”), is because the waving is to halt evil winds and harmful dews, and to rebuke Satan. Therefore, one must wave the during the verse Ana Adonai hoshia na; that is, "save us from these harms." But during Ana Hashem hatzlicha na, this reasoning does not apply. But the Hiddushei Devash offers a different explanation. It is because the two statements are a single verse, and one does not wave two times for the same verse. 20 See Psalm 118:25 where the two statements appear together in a single verse: “אָנָּ֣א ה' הוֹשִׁ֘יעָ֥ה נָּ֑א אָנָּ֥א ה' הַצְלִ֘יחָ֥ה נָּֽא׃ In Sefer HaTashbetz, the author brings scriptural support (an asmachta) for why we wave for Ana Adonai hoshia na and not for Ana Hashem hatzlicha na, from the verse, “Then shall all the trees of the forest sing,” (I Chr. 16:33) 21i class=''footnote''>Sefer Tanchuma Emor S.18 and afterward, Hodu, “Praise YHVH, for He is good, God’s steadfast love is eternal.” They said, Hoshee’aynu, ‘Save us.' (I Chr. 16:34-25). The Midrash teaches: On Rosh Hashanah, Israel and the nations of the world come before judgment, and it is not known who will emerge acquitted and who will emerge liable. The Holy One gave this commandment to Israel so they would rejoice with their lulavim like a person who departs from before the judge vindicated. As is written, “Then shall all trees of the forest shout for joy before the Lord.” (I Chr. 16:33) That is to say, they rejoice with the trees of the forest when they go out before God, vindicated when God judges the earth. How do they rejoice? They do so with Hodu and with Hoshee’ayunu The Rosh writes, Now since it is the custom for the prayer leader to יֹֽאמַר־נָ֥א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ “Let Israel declare, ‘God’s steadfast love is forever,’” (Ps. 118:2) and the community responds, הוֹד֣וּ…כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ “Praise Adonai for God is God God’s steadfast love is forever” (Ps. 118:1) , and similarly the prayer leader says יֹֽאמְרוּ־נָ֥א בֵֽית־אַהֲרֹ֑ן כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ, “Let the house of Aaron say, ‘God’s steadfast love is forever’” (Ps. 118:3) and “יֹֽאמְרוּ־נָ֭א יִרְאֵ֣י….כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ “Let those who fear Adonai say, ‘God’s steadfast love is forever.’” (Ps. 118:4) The community waves the lulav and etrog for each hodu, Until here. But this is not the general custom of the world.
